With a fire barrier wall, offset distances to Exposure Groups 1 and 2 can be reduced by 50%, and Exposure Group 3 distances can be reduced to 0 ft (NFPA 2, Section 8.3.2.3.1.6(C)). As LH demand scales above 10 MTPD at an airport, on-site liquefaction becomes more viable. 2 However, the spatial footprint of the liquefaction plant must be considered before the airport can make a final investment decision. Argonne National Laboratory notes in HDSAM that the spatial footprint for a standard 30 MTPD liquefier is 25,000 m2 (which equates to a square with side length of nearly 520 ft) equivalent to 0.83 m2 per kilogram of LH produced each day, and scales 2 according to a 0.6 exponential factor (i.e., 10-MTPD liquefier = 13,000-m2 footprint) (Argonne National Laboratory n.d.). If an airport is considering producing its own hydrogen, this will also take up space. Refer to Table 7 for information on hydrogen production technologies and their potential spatial footprint. Given the nascency of hydrogen-powered aviation and aircraft hydrogen demand projections mentioned in Section 4.4.1, it is expected that aircraft LH consumption at most airports would 2 remain on the order of 10 MTPD or less by 2050. Therefore, liquid hydrogen trucking is likely to be the primary delivery method for the next few decades as demand scales, and the LH storage 2 systems and dispensing infrastructure will be the primary space consumers. More detail on integrating these other hydrogen applications at airports can be found in NLR’s report titled Hydrogen Applications for Energy Transition in Port and Airport Operations at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey (Semchukova et al. 2025). 4.3.1.3 Distribution and Dispensing Configurations, Operations, and Procedures As mentioned in Section 4.2.1.4, possible distribution and dispensing methods of LH include 1) 2 fixed refueling directly next to the bulk storage system, 2) mobile refuelers, 3) liquid hydrogen distribution pipelines from the bulk storage to hydrant refueling points and 4) swappable tanks. In this subsection we explore these configurations in more detail and mention notable safety considerations and operational procedures that will require further specification before the technology is commercially established. Fixed refueling directly next to bulk storage systems would occur on the airport tarmac and is likely to leverage LH pumps with insulated transfer lines. Importantly, this configuration would 2 require finding a location for bulk LH storage that is directly adjacent to the tarmac such that the 2 aircraft and storage tanks are within a reasonable distance from each other while also meeting separation distance requirements yet to determined.
